intro_what: An OpenAI-compatible security gateway for AI agents. Tool results, fetched pages, MCP payloads and RAG chunks pass through spanguard before the agent reads them; validated rules, a 135M-parameter multilingual span model and a 0.79M char-level multi-task model find prompt-injection text inside the data and replace each span with [stripped], while orders, totals, names and JSON structure survive untouched. The fast-v2 ensemble gates the detectors by document structure: high-recall union on tool output, corroboration on prose.
intro_alternative: The strongest open binary guard on the same set (horizon injection-guard base, strip-all semantics) reaches 6.2% escape only by over-stripping 59.0% of benign characters — the agent loses most of what it was reading; protectai deberta-v3 is worse than spanguard on BOTH axes (35.4% escape, 71.8% over-strip); a 0.5B LLM asked to flag its own injections misses 91.7% of attacks. spanguard's char-only tier trades a further escape cut (4.2%) for 18.3% over-strip when security outweighs data fidelity.
intro_measured: Committed run records per system and set (eval/results/), fictional data only, an external public set for generalization, per-attack-family heatmaps, CPU latency measured where each system ran, and a cost ledger. Rerun everything with `make eval` + the Kaggle kernels in training/train/.
latency_note: p50 latency per document, measured where each system ran (records carry p50/p95): rules 0.2 ms, spanguard fast (135M span model, CPU 2 threads) 277 ms, spanguard char (0.79M) ~2 ms, horizon-small (binary, strip-all) 87.5 ms, protectai deberta 253.5 ms; the LLM self-detect column includes local generation time. Latency is the honest cost of span-level multilingual detection on CPU; spanguard-char is the sub-ms tier when that matters more than escape rate.
cost_note: LLM-based guarding pays per token; local guards pay $0 per document — computed from recorded token usage at Baseten list prices
